title: Principle 8: Intuition: Dig deep before building up
hook: Negative numbers in a spreadsheet can expose a formula nobody really understands.
counterintuition: Intuition is not speed piled on top of shallow fluency, but the patience to stop at the fragile step and explain why it works before adding more.
tryThisNow: Find one step you can perform but cannot explain, then ask why it works until you reach a concrete cause.
keyTakeaway: Build intuition by pausing at shallow fluency, digging into why the step works, and returning that understanding to the real performance.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beatrice sees an unexpected negative number in a spreadsheet cell. The macro still runs, but the exception makes no sense. She can click again and hope the output clears, or she can trace the formula until she can explain why the number appears.

Intuition is not a feeling of cleverness. It is understanding deep enough to survive a changed case. Adding more material on top of a weak explanation only builds higher on a soft floor.

Stop where the step works but your explanation does not.
breakdown.deepRead:
Ryan sits at a seminar table with one highlighted sentence folded in the handout. His explanation sounded smooth until a classmate asked why the claim followed from the evidence. The sentence stayed in his memory. The support underneath did not.

That is shallow fluency pretending to be intuition.

Surface familiarity can carry a learner through repeated examples. It fails when the shape changes. Digging deep means pausing before more pages, more cards, or more procedures, and asking what makes the current step true. The answer should change how the next case looks.

Etienne learns this with a capsule diagram beside a pharmacy case note. More flashcards would increase volume, but the drug mechanism still feels like a label. He follows the mechanism through one patient case before adding new cards. The result is slower for an hour and stronger later.

Depth should return to performance. If explanation becomes a private theory hobby, it has wandered. The test is whether the deeper grasp changes the next problem, patient, climb, bowl, or spreadsheet.

Beatrice sees the same pattern in the negative spreadsheet cell. The macro still runs, so the easy move is to rerun it and trust the output. Instead, she follows the formula through the exception until the sign error makes sense. The work slows down for ten minutes, but the next report becomes safer because she now understands the cause, not only the button.
breakdown.fullRead:
Catarina stands under a climbing hold marked in chalk just above the mat. A student keeps falling on the same balance transfer. Catarina can describe the move, but when the student asks why the hip has to shift before the foot, her answer thins out.

"Show me why," the student says.

Catarina steps onto the wall and feels the missing explanation in her own body. The breakdown is small, but it reveals a real gap. She does not need a motivational speech or a larger catalog of drills. She needs to understand the balance transfer deeply enough to coach it when the hold angle changes.

What can you do correctly but not explain when the conditions change?

That question finds the place where intuition should begin. A learner can repeat a procedure, quote a sentence, run a macro, solve a familiar problem, or demonstrate a movement without knowing why it works. That is useful at first. It becomes dangerous when more material gets stacked on top. The higher layers depend on a lower layer that cannot answer back.

Akira sees the same problem in statistics. At 9:10 p.m., a scatterplot with one outlier circled in black sits beside the next problem set. He predicts more pages will make the concept settle. Then the next problem changes shape, and the old explanation no longer fits. He slows down on one core concept until he can say why the outlier changes the interpretation, not merely which formula to apply.

Changed cases are the pressure test for intuition. If the explanation only works when the example is identical, it is still tied to surface familiarity. When the shape changes and the cause still guides the next move, understanding has started to travel.

There is a limit. Digging deep is not an excuse to avoid practice. Understanding should reconnect to the real skill. Beatrice traces the formula so the spreadsheet decision improves. Catarina explains balance so the student climbs better. Akira digs into the concept so new problems become readable. The proof of depth is not how elaborate the explanation sounds; it is what the next attempt can now do.

Anke learns this at the wheel. A clay bowl collapses on one side, and her theory notes say pressure and centering in tidy words. In the postmortem, she brings the idea back to the wet clay and changes hand pressure on the next attempt. The explanation becomes useful only when the bowl changes.

Dig until the step can survive a new shape. Then build higher.

The practical test is simple: can the idea survive a change in shape? If the formula only works when the numbers look familiar, the understanding is still shallow. If the climbing cue only works on one wall angle, Catarina has a performance trick, not intuition. Digging deep means changing the example, the case, or the object until the explanation either holds or breaks. A break is not failure. It is the door into real understanding.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet macro gives a surprising negative number two days before month-end. What should Beatrice do before running it again? The next choice will decide whether today's work produces evidence or only another round of comfort.
choices: Trace the formula and explain why the exception appears.
Add more macros so the report has backup outputs.
Ignore the exception because the macro usually works.
questions.explanation: Tracing the formula builds causal understanding of the exception. More macros add surface machinery, and ignoring the surprise leaves the weak explanation intact.

questions.prompt: Ryan can recite a seminar claim but stalls when asked why the evidence supports it. What is missing? A reviewer will see the result tomorrow, so the answer must choose an action rather than a preference.
choices: A smoother sentence to memorize.
The support underneath the claim.
A cleaner page of notes.
questions.explanation: The why question exposes the missing support. Memorizing a smoother sentence or rewriting notes would polish the surface while the argument stays hollow.

questions.prompt: Etienne wants more drug flashcards, but one mechanism still feels like a label. What should come next? The deadline is close enough that extra preparation would hide the weakness instead of testing it.
choices: Collect more drug names before using cases.
Avoid cases until every term feels familiar.
Follow that mechanism through a patient case.
questions.explanation: The patient case forces the mechanism to explain something. More labels would stack facts on shallow grasp, and avoiding cases delays the real test.

questions.prompt: A climbing coach can demonstrate a balance move but cannot explain it when a hold angle changes. What should she do? A real artifact is waiting on the table, and the learner needs a move that changes the next attempt.
choices: Rebuild the explanation from the changed movement on the wall.
Add more generic drills for the student.
Tell the student to copy the demonstration silently.
questions.explanation: The changed hold exposes the gap, so explanation must return to the movement. Generic drills and silent copying avoid the missing cause.

questions.prompt: A statistics problem changes shape and Akira’s memorized formula cue fails. What is the depth move? Limited time remains before review, so the best option should expose the skill gap quickly.
choices: Search for a more familiar example only.
Explain why the concept applies before doing more pages.
Skip the concept and continue the problem set.
questions.explanation: A changed problem tests whether the concept is understood. More familiar examples may soothe recognition, and skipping the concept leaves the weak layer untouched.

questions.prompt: A ceramics instructor has tidy notes about pressure, but the next bowl collapses. What would test understanding? Yesterday's visible miss is still on the page, so the response should use that evidence.
choices: Rewrite the notes in cleaner language.
Stay away from the wheel until the theory feels complete.
Apply the explanation at the wheel and change hand pressure on the next attempt.
questions.explanation: The wheel is where the theory must work. Cleaner notes may help later, but only the next bowl shows whether the explanation changes performance.

questions.prompt: Why can adding more material on top of shallow grasp weaken later learning? The learner can protect the old habit or make the next attempt more honest under pressure.
choices: Later material depends on a lower layer that cannot explain changed cases.
More material always reduces motivation.
Shallow grasp is fine if the learner moves quickly.
questions.explanation: Weak lower understanding makes later topics brittle. The issue is not motivation or speed alone, but a foundation that cannot answer why.

questions.prompt: Which sign best shows intuition is forming? One session remains before feedback, and the answer should choose the useful constraint.
choices: The learner can repeat the same example faster.
The learner can explain a step and use that explanation in a changed case.
The learner has collected many notes about the topic.
questions.explanation: Intuition travels to changed cases. Speed on identical examples and large note collections can still hide surface familiarity.

questions.prompt: A learner spends hours explaining concepts but never lets the explanation change real practice. What boundary has been crossed? The choice matters because the next attempt will be judged by output, not by how effortful it felt.
choices: The learner has mastered intuition.
Practice should now be abandoned for more explanation.
Depth work has drifted into theory detached from the skill.
questions.explanation: Understanding should reconnect to performance. Detached explanation may feel deep, but it no longer improves the task it was meant to support.

reviewCards.front: A learner can perform a step but cannot explain why it works. What does that reveal?
reviewCards.back: You can repeat the step, but a why question or changed case makes the explanation collapse.

reviewCards.front: What should happen before adding more material?
reviewCards.back: Pause at the fragile step and explain why it works in a way that changes the next attempt.

reviewCards.front: Why is depth not theory for its own sake?
reviewCards.back: The explanation must reconnect to the real skill: the case, wall, bowl, spreadsheet, or problem.

reviewCards.front: A learner keeps adding facts after a why question fails. What risk is growing?
reviewCards.back: Later material rests on a weak layer, so changed cases become harder to interpret.
Change the problem shape and see whether the explanation still guides action.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is depth before build-up. You stop at a step you can perform but cannot explain, dig into why it works, and return that explanation to the real task.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a tool output surprises you before a deadline, then trace the cause in one small case before running the tool again.
If a memorized sentence fails a why question, then rebuild the support with one example before adding new notes.
If a mechanism feels like a label during case review, then follow it through one patient case before making more cards.
If theory sounds right but the object fails in practice, then test the explanation in the next physical attempt and adjust one cause.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one step you can perform but cannot explain, then ask why it works until you reach a concrete cause.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, choose one familiar move and test whether your explanation survives a changed case.
